title: Biological Classification
tagline: From Aristotle to Whittaker: five kingdoms, and the acellular organisms that sit outside all of them.

overview.intro: Classification is the biological answer to a practical problem: how to name, group and then predict an organism when millions of kinds exist. This chapter traces the principles that make classification possible — similarity, divergence and the newer evidence from ultrastructure and molecular sequences — works through the five-kingdom scheme that organises every living thing taught in this course, and then treats the two groups that a five-kingdom scheme still has to explain separately, viruses and viroids, which are not cells at all. The examination pattern is consistent: a compare-the-kingdoms table, a question on the reasons for placing an organism in a particular kingdom, and one on why viruses are called acellular.

facts.value: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, separated by cell structure, nutrition and body organisation.

learningOutcomes: State the principles of classification and explain binomial nomenclature with its rules.
Compare the five kingdoms on cell type, nutrition, body organisation and reproduction.
Classify Monera by shape, cell wall and mode of nutrition, and give the economic and medical roles of bacteria.
Describe viruses, viroids and lichens, and justify why each is placed as it is.
Apply the criteria of classification to an unfamiliar organism and place it correctly with reasons.

blocks.text: Classification arranges living organisms into a hierarchy of groups — kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus and species — so that an organism placed in a group shares features with the others in it. The principles behind the arrangement have changed with the evidence. Aristotle classified plants by the degree of woodiness of their stems and animals by whether they lived in water or on land, a useful but artificial scheme. The natural system of classification, developed through the nineteenth century, groups organisms by all available similarities, both external and internal, so that the grouping predicts relationship. Modern systems add chemical and molecular evidence: the comparison of 16S ribosomal RNA sequences, the base composition of DNA and the ultrastructure visible in the electron microscope now decide relationships that morphology alone left uncertain. Nomenclature fixes the result in language. Binomial nomenclature, introduced by Linnaeus, gives every organism a two-part name in which the first word is the generic name and must begin with a capital letter and the second the specific epithet, always in lower case; both parts are italicised when printed, or underlined separately when written, and the name is followed by the name of the describer in full scientific writing. The rules of priority govern disputes: the earliest legitimate name for a taxon is the accepted one, which is why many familiar organisms have synonyms that specialists must check.

items: Hierarchy: kingdom, phylum or division, class, order, family, genus, species, with each step narrowing the shared features.
Artificial schemes use one or two convenient characters; natural schemes use all available similarities, external and internal.
Modern classification adds ultrastructure, chemical composition and nucleic acid sequences to morphology.
Binomial nomenclature: genus capitalised, species lower case, italicised when printed and underlined separately when written.
A change of name requires a published reason and the rules of priority, so that only the earliest valid name stands.
The purpose of naming is unambiguous communication: one name for one organism everywhere in the world.

blocks.caption: Ranks of classification, largest to smallest
rows: organisms able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring

items.note: The house crow is written Corvus splendens, with Corvus capitalised as the genus and splendens lower case as the specific epithet, both underlined separately when handwritten.
Several plant names were altered when molecular work moved a species into a different genus; the older synonym remains in older literature, which is why priority rules exist.

items.meaning: The science of classification, nomenclature and identification of organisms.
A group of similar organisms able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
The two-part system of naming in which genus and species are written together as one name.
Classification based on all available similarities rather than on a single convenient character.

blocks.text: Whittaker’s five-kingdom scheme sorts life by four criteria taken together: the type of cells, whether they have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; the mode of nutrition, whether the organism makes its own food, absorbs dissolved material or ingests it; the body organisation, from loose aggregation through tissues to organs and systems; and how the organisms reproduce and relate to one another. Kingdom Monera holds the prokaryotes — cells without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles — which includes all bacteria and the cyanobacteria; they may be autotrophic or heterotrophic, unicellular or filamentous, and their cell wall is made of peptidoglycan. Kingdom Protista holds the eukaryotic organisms that are not clearly plants, animals or fungi: the protozoa, which are animal-like and ingest their food, the algae, which are plant-like and photosynthetic, and the slime moulds and water moulds, which feed on decaying matter. Kingdom Fungi holds eukaryotic absorptive heterotrophs with cell walls of chitin, organised as thread-like hyphae that form a network, the mycelium. Kingdom Plantae holds multicellular photosynthetic autotrophs with cell walls of cellulose and a body differentiated into organs. Kingdom Animalia holds multicellular heterotrophs that ingest their food, with no cell walls and a body organised into tissues, organs and systems. The scheme also places viruses outside all five kingdoms, because they have no cellular structure at all.

items: Monera: prokaryotic cells, no nucleus, peptidoglycan cell wall, nutrition by absorption or autotrophy, unicellular or filamentous.
Protista: eukaryotic, mostly unicellular, aquatic, nutrition by ingestion, photosynthesis or absorption.
Fungi: eukaryotic, cell wall of chitin, body of hyphae forming a mycelium, nutrition by absorption using secreted enzymes.
Plantae: multicellular, cellulose cell wall, photosynthetic, with alternation of generations in most groups.
Animalia: multicellular, no cell wall, ingestive nutrition, tissues and organs, mostly motile at some stage.
Viruses fall outside the kingdoms because they are acellular: nucleic acid inside a protein coat and nothing else.

blocks.caption: The five kingdoms compared
rows: cells into tissues, organs and systems

items.note: They feed like animals on decaying matter yet form a body like a fungus when starving, so the intermediate features place them with the Protista.
Yeast is unicellular, yet its chitin-containing wall and absorptive nutrition place it in Fungi rather than Protista — a reminder that cell wall chemistry and nutrition outrank cell number.

learn.title: Kingdom Monera: bacteria, their forms and their roles

blocks.text: Bacteria are the dominant prokaryotes and the most numerous organisms on Earth, and their classification begins with shape: cocci are spherical, and may appear in pairs as diplococci, in chains as streptococci or in grape-like clusters as staphylococci; bacilli are rod-shaped; spirilla are spiral; and vibrio are comma-shaped. Their cell wall, made of peptidoglycan, lies outside a plasma membrane, and many carry extra DNA in the form of a plasmid, a small circular molecule that can be transferred between cells and often carries resistance to antibiotics. Some produce endospores, thick-walled resting forms that survive boiling, drying and radiation, which is why sterilisation rather than ordinary cleaning is needed in a laboratory. Nutrition ranges from autotrophy — photosynthetic bacteria and cyanobacteria — to saprozoic absorption of dissolved food, and a few are parasitic. A specialised group, the archaea, shares the prokaryotic plan yet differs in membrane chemistry and in the sequences of its ribosomal RNA, and thrives in hot springs, salt lakes and other extreme habitats. Economically the group is indispensable: Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the roots of legumes, Lactobacillus sours milk into curd and yoghurt, Acetobacter produces vinegar, and Streptomyces supplies the antibiotic streptomycin; medically, bacteria cause tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, plague and wound infections, and the study of their transmission is what founded the germ theory of disease.

items: Shapes: cocci in pairs, chains or clusters; bacilli rods; spirilla spirals; vibrio commas.
Structure: cell wall of peptidoglycan, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleoid with the main chromosome, plasmids and sometimes pili and flagella.
Endospores are resistant resting forms that survive conditions lethal to the vegetative cell.
Nutrition: photosynthetic autotrophy, saprozoic absorption, or parasitic absorption from a host.
Archaea are prokaryotes with distinct membrane chemistry and RNA sequences, often living in extreme habitats.
Useful bacteria: Rhizobium in nitrogen fixation, Lactobacillus in curd, Acetobacter in vinegar, Streptomyces giving streptomycin.
Harmful bacteria: the agents of tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, plague and septic infection.

items.note: Streptococcus grows in chains that break apart easily, so the organisms pass from person to person through droplets and contact with remarkable efficiency.
Bacteria carrying plasmids for antibiotic resistance pass those plasmids to other bacteria, which is why one infection may need a change of antibiotic.

blocks.text: Viruses sit outside the five kingdoms because they are not made of cells. A typical virus consists of nucleic acid — either DNA or RNA, and in a given virus never both — enclosed in a protein coat called the capsid, and some carry an outer envelope derived from the host cell membrane studded with attachment proteins. They have no cytoplasm, no organelles, no ribosomes and no independent metabolism, so outside a living host they are inert crystals, while inside a host they hijack the cell’s machinery to copy themselves, a habit that makes them obligate intracellular parasites. Sizes range from the small polio and tobacco mosaic viruses to the large bacteriophages that infect bacteria, and the shape varies with the group: polyhedral, helical, or a complex head-and-tail form. The disease list is well known — smallpox, influenza, polio, rabies, AIDS, hepatitis, dengue and the common cold — and treatment relies on vaccines and on antiviral drugs, since antibiotics have no effect on viruses. Viroids are smaller and simpler still: naked RNA molecules with no protein coat, which cause plant diseases such as potato spindle tuber disease by interfering with the host’s own RNA processing. Prions are a third oddity, infectious proteins with no nucleic acid at all, which cause spongiform encephalopathies such as scrapie and mad cow disease. Lichens, by contrast, are not parasites but a stable symbiosis: a fungal partner that provides the body and absorbs water and minerals, and a photosynthetic partner — a green alga or a cyanobacterium — that supplies carbohydrates, so that lichens can colonise bare rock and begin the formation of soil.

items: Viruses: nucleic acid plus protein capsid, sometimes an envelope, with no cytoplasm or organelles.
A virus carries DNA or RNA, never both, and reproduces only inside a living host cell.
Shapes: polyhedral, helical, and the complex head-and-tail form of bacteriophages.
Viral diseases of humans include smallpox, influenza, polio, rabies, AIDS, hepatitis and dengue; antibiotics do not act on them.
Viroids are naked infectious RNA without a protein coat and cause plant diseases such as potato spindle tuber disease.
Prions are infectious proteins with no nucleic acid, causing spongiform encephalopathies.
Lichens are a symbiosis of a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium, and they colonise bare rock to start soil formation.

blocks.caption: Virus, viroid and prion compared
rows: the infectious agent itself is protein

items.note: Rod-shaped particles of RNA in a helical capsid mosaic the leaves of tobacco, which was the first virus to be isolated and gives the group its name.
Grey-green crusts on bare rock are a fungus and an alga living together, slowly dissolving the stone and building the first thin layer of soil.

items.meaning: The protein coat that surrounds the nucleic acid of a virus.
An organism that can reproduce only inside the cells of a host, as viruses do.
A naked RNA molecule, without a protein coat, that causes disease in plants.
A stable symbiotic association of a fungus with a green alga or cyanobacterium.

learn.title: Applying classification: the method that earns marks

blocks.text: Questions that ask where an organism belongs are answered by working through the criteria in a fixed order rather than by recalling a list. Ask first whether there is a membrane-bound nucleus: no places the organism in Monera, yes takes it to the eukaryotic kingdoms. Ask second whether the organism is unicellular, colonial or multicellular, since unicellular eukaryotes are Protista. If it is multicellular, ask how it obtains food: photosynthesis with a cellulose wall places it in Plantae; absorption with a chitin wall places it in Fungi; ingestion without a cell wall places it in Animalia. Any organism that has no cellular structure at all — a virus, a viroid, a prion — is outside the kingdoms entirely and must be described rather than placed. Two habits finish the answer. Quote the character as well as the kingdom, because the mark is for the reasoning, not for the label: writing Fungi earns little, while writing Fungi because the wall is of chitin and nutrition is absorptive through secreted enzymes earns all of it. And check the exceptions that examiners like: yeast is a fungus despite being unicellular, slime moulds are Protista despite forming fungus-like bodies, and Euglena is Protista despite having chloroplasts because it can also ingest food.

items: Order the questions: nucleus present? unicellular or multicellular? how is food obtained? what is the cell wall made of?
No nucleus means Monera; no cellular structure at all means outside the kingdoms.
Multicellular with cellulose wall and photosynthesis means Plantae; chitin wall and absorption means Fungi; no wall and ingestion means Animalia.
Quote the deciding character alongside the kingdom — the reasoning carries the marks.
Know the exceptions: yeast is a fungus, slime moulds are Protista, Euglena is Protista.
Give the basis of your placement explicitly whenever the question asks for reasons.

items.text: A unicellular organism with chloroplasts and a cellulose wall
items.note: It photosynthesises, has a nucleus and is unicellular: kingdom Protista, since the photosynthetic members of that kingdom are the algae.

items.text: A filamentous organism with chitin walls absorbing sugar from dead wood
items.note: Chitin and absorption place it in Fungi, and the filaments are hyphae which together form the mycelium of the fruiting body.

keyPoints: Classification groups organisms by shared features so that membership predicts relationship.
Modern classification adds ultrastructure, chemistry and nucleic acid sequences to morphology.
Binomial nomenclature gives a genus capitalised and a species in lower case, italicised or underlined separately.
The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
The kingdoms separate on cell type, mode of nutrition, body organisation and reproduction.
Monera are prokaryotes with cell walls of peptidoglycan; many are decomposers and some fix nitrogen.
Bacteria are classified by shape: cocci, bacilli, spirilla and vibrio.
Fungi have chitin walls and absorptive nutrition through secreted enzymes.
Viruses are acellular: nucleic acid in a protein capsid, reproducing only inside a host cell.
A virus contains DNA or RNA but never both, and antibiotics have no effect on it.
Viroids are naked infectious RNA; prions are infectious proteins without nucleic acid.
Lichens are a symbiosis of a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium and begin soil formation on bare rock.
examFocus: Kingdom comparison questions want the table form: cells, nutrition, body organisation, reproduction.
Placement questions must quote the deciding character alongside the kingdom name.
The virus question expects the acellular argument with the list of what viruses lack.
Quote at least one useful and one harmful example for bacteria in any long answer.

vocabulary.meaning: The science of classifying, naming and identifying organisms.
A group that interbreeds to produce fertile offspring.
A cell without a membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
The polymer that gives bacterial cell walls their structure.
The network of hyphae that makes up the body of a fungus.
The protein shell enclosing a virus’s nucleic acid.
A naked RNA infectious agent of plants with no protein coat.
A close and lasting association between two different organisms, as in a lichen.

questions.prompt: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom scheme in 1969 on the criteria of cell structure, nutrition and body organisation.

questions.prompt: Which kingdom includes organisms whose cell walls are made of chitin?
questions.explanation: Chitin is the characteristic wall material of fungi, distinguishing them from the cellulose walls of plants.

questions.prompt: A virus that infects bacteria is called a:
questions.explanation: Bacteriophages are the viruses that infect bacteria, with a characteristic head-and-tail structure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT found in a virus?
questions.explanation: Viruses lack ribosomes and every other organelle, which is why they cannot make proteins outside a host cell.

questions.prompt: The two-part name of an organism consists of the genus and the __________ epithet.
questions.explanation: The genus is capitalised and the species is written entirely in lower case.

questions.prompt: Naked infectious RNA without a protein coat, which causes plant disease, is called a __________.
questions.explanation: Viroids are smaller than viruses and were first isolated from potato spindle tuber disease.

questions.prompt: State the four criteria used to separate the five kingdoms.
questions.answer: The first criterion is cell type, whether the cells are prokaryotic or eukaryotic and whether a membrane-bound nucleus is present. The second is mode of nutrition, distinguishing autotrophic, absorptive and ingestive feeding. The third is body organisation, ranging from unicellular or simple colonies through hyphal networks to tissues, organs and organ systems. The fourth is the way organisms reproduce and their patterns of cell-to-cell contact, which separates the kingdoms at the level of life cycle and development.
questions.explanation: Cell type, nutrition, body organisation and reproduction or life cycle, each explained in a line.

questions.prompt: Give the rules of binomial nomenclature and one reason why it is needed.
questions.answer: Every organism is given a two-part name: the generic name, which begins with a capital letter, followed by the specific epithet, which is written entirely in lower case. When printed, both parts are italicised; when handwritten, each part is underlined separately. The name is not abbreviated, a change requires a published reason under the rules of priority, and the system gives one universal name to each organism so that workers in different countries refer to the same species without confusion.
questions.explanation: Capitalisation, lower case, printing and underlining rules, plus the reason for a universal system.

questions.prompt: What are endospores and why do they matter practically?
questions.answer: Endospores are thick-walled, resistant resting structures formed by certain bacteria such as Bacillus and Clostridium when conditions become unfavourable. They survive boiling, drying, radiation and disinfectants, and germinate into vegetative cells when conditions improve. Practically they matter because an ordinary disinfectant will not sterilise a culture or an instrument that carries endospores: heat under pressure or prolonged incineration is needed to destroy them.
questions.explanation: Thick-walled resistant resting form, the conditions it survives, and the sterilisation consequence.

questions.prompt: Compare Kingdom Monera with Kingdom Fungi, and explain why they are placed in different kingdoms.
questions.answer: Monera and Fungi differ most fundamentally in cell type. Monera are prokaryotic: their cells have no membrane-bound nucleus, the genetic material lies in a nucleoid, there are no membrane-bound organelles, and the cell wall is made of peptidoglycan. Fungi are eukaryotic: the nucleus is enclosed in a nuclear envelope, mitochondria and other organelles are present, and the cell wall is made of chitin. Nutrition differs as well. Monera include autotrophs such as cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria as well as organisms that absorb dissolved food, whereas fungi are exclusively absorptive heterotrophs that secrete enzymes into their surroundings and take up the products. Organisation also separates them: monerans are unicellular or form simple filaments without true branching septa, while fungi form a well-defined mycelium of branching hyphae which may build large fruiting bodies. Finally, their life cycles differ — fungi show alternation of haploid and diploid phases with a dikaryotic stage, while monerans divide simply by binary fission. These differences in cell architecture, nutrition, body plan and reproduction are why a single kingdom cannot hold both.
questions.explanation: Both kingdoms covered under cell type, nutrition, organisation and life cycle, with a closing sentence naming the differences that justify the separation.

questions.prompt: A microorganism is observed to have no nucleus, a cell wall of peptidoglycan, it lives in soil and decomposes dead plant material, and it forms a thick-walled structure when conditions dry out. Place it in a kingdom and justify each observed feature.
questions.answer: The absence of a membrane-bound nucleus places the organism in Kingdom Monera, since that is the defining prokaryotic condition and separates it from every other kingdom. The peptidoglycan cell wall confirms the placement, because this polymer is characteristic of bacteria and is absent from fungi, plants and animals. Saprotrophic nutrition on dead plant material is common in Monera, where decomposers break down organic matter and return minerals to the soil, and it fits the absorptive nutrition of the group. The thick-walled structure formed in dry conditions is an endospore, a resistant resting form typical of genera such as Bacillus, which survives desiccation and heat until conditions improve. Each observation therefore points to the same conclusion: a soil bacterium of Kingdom Monera, whose combination of prokaryotic cell, bacterial wall, decomposer nutrition and endospore formation leaves no other kingdom possible.
questions.explanation: Each feature addressed in turn with the reasoning that links it to Monera, and a closing statement that the features converge.

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses are not included in the five-kingdom classification, and describe their structure and reproduction.
questions.answer: The five kingdoms are built from cellular criteria — the presence of a nucleus, the nature of the cell wall, the mode of nutrition of a cell, and the organisation of cells into tissues or colonies — and a virus fails the first requirement altogether because it is not made of cells. Its structure is a piece of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA but never both, surrounded by a protein capsid, with an additional lipid envelope in some animal viruses; it has no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no energy metabolism of its own. Reproduction is therefore impossible outside a living host: the virus attaches to a specific cell using its attachment proteins, its nucleic acid enters and takes over the cell’s machinery, new viral parts are assembled, and the cell bursts to release the new viruses. Because the virus has no cell structure, no independent metabolism and no mode of nutrition, none of the criteria that define a kingdom applies to it, so it is described separately as an acellular infectious agent rather than being placed in Monera or any other kingdom.
questions.explanation: The acellular argument against the kingdom criteria, the structure with nucleic acid and capsid, and the intracellular reproduction cycle.
